titulo: Drought, farming and the economics of water in southern Europe

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: On a hot morning in late summer, the reservoir that supplies a small town in Andalusia looks more like a desert than a lake. Cracked mud stretches for hundreds of metres, and the ruins of an old village, flooded decades ago, have reappeared above the surface. Local farmers come to look at it the way people visit a sick relative. For them, the falling water level is not a picturesque curiosity but a direct threat to their livelihoods.

Scenes like this have become familiar across southern Europe. In recent years Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece have suffered long periods of drought, with rainfall well below average and record temperatures. Some regions, such as Catalonia, were forced to impose strict restrictions on water use, and in certain places drinking water had to be brought in by ship or by lorry. Although heavy rains later refilled many reservoirs, scientists warn that such episodes will become more frequent and more intense as the climate warms.

Agriculture sits at the heart of the problem. In Spain, as in much of the Mediterranean, farming uses around three-quarters or more of all the water consumed, mainly for irrigation. Irrigated land represents a minority of the cultivated area, but it produces a large share of the value of agricultural output. Fruit, vegetables, olives and almonds grown in the south and east of the country are exported all over Europe, and the sector supports many jobs in rural areas where alternatives are scarce.

This success has a cost. Over the past decades, the area under irrigation has expanded significantly, often encouraged by public subsidies and by the conversion of traditional dry crops into more profitable irrigated ones. In some areas, farmers have drilled wells illegally and pumped groundwater faster than nature can replace it. The case of Doñana, one of Europe’s most important wetlands, has become a symbol of this tension: scientists have repeatedly warned that the extraction of water for nearby strawberry farms is drying up its lagoons.

One farmer, who grows oranges and lemons a few kilometres from the coast, explains the dilemma. ‘We have invested in drip irrigation, sensors and everything the experts recommended,’ he says. ‘We use much less water per tree than my father did. But when the authorities cut our allocation by half, efficiency is not enough. You cannot keep a tree alive with good intentions.’ His frustration is shared by many in the sector, who feel they are being blamed for a crisis caused by the weather.

Economists point to an uncomfortable paradox. Modern irrigation techniques save water on each plot, but the savings are often used to expand the irrigated area or to switch to thirstier crops, so total consumption does not fall. This phenomenon, known as the rebound effect, has been observed in several regions. Without firm limits on the total amount of water that can be used, they argue, technology alone cannot solve the problem and may even make it worse.

At the centre of the debate is the price of water. In many parts of southern Europe, farmers pay only a fraction of the real cost of the water they use, including the cost of building dams and canals and the damage caused to rivers and aquifers. Low prices encourage waste and make it difficult to direct water to the uses that create the most value. Some experts propose water markets, in which users can buy and sell rights, as in parts of Australia and California. Critics fear that such markets would favour large companies over small family farms.

Other solutions focus on increasing supply. Spain is already one of the world’s leading users of desalination, and new plants are being built along the Mediterranean coast. Desalinated water, however, requires large amounts of energy and remains more expensive than water from rivers, although the growth of cheap solar power may change the calculation. The reuse of treated wastewater for irrigation is another option, still underused in many countries despite European rules designed to encourage it.

Transfers of water between river basins, a traditional solution in Spain, are increasingly controversial. Regions that send water complain that they are losing a resource they need for their own future, while those that receive it argue that their farms and jobs depend on it. These disputes have a strong political dimension and frequently end up in court. In a warmer climate, with less water to share, they are likely to become even more bitter.

The European Union is also involved. Its water rules require member states to bring rivers and aquifers into good condition, and part of the subsidies paid under the common agricultural policy is linked to environmental requirements. Brussels has repeatedly criticised Spain for failing to protect certain wetlands. At the same time, European consumers continue to demand cheap fruit and vegetables all year round, which, in a sense, means importing water from the driest regions of the continent.

Back at the reservoir, the farmers know that the future will not look like the past. Some are already experimenting with crops that need less water, such as pistachios or hardier varieties of olive, and with techniques that protect the soil from evaporation. Others fear that their children will simply abandon the land. Whether southern Europe can preserve a dynamic agriculture with less water will depend on difficult choices about prices, rights and priorities, choices that can no longer be postponed until the next rain.
titulo_es: Sequía, agricultura y economía del agua en el sur de Europa
resumen_es: Reportaje sobre cómo las sequías ponen en tensión el regadío en el sur de Europa y sobre las respuestas posibles: precio del agua, mercados, desalación, reutilización y trasvases.

ideas_clave.idea: Repeated droughts in southern European countries are threatening farmers’ incomes, and climate change is expected to make them more frequent.
Irrigated farming consumes most of the water in Spain but generates much of the value of farm output and of rural employment.
The expansion of irrigation, sometimes through illegal wells, has overexploited aquifers, as the case of Doñana shows.
Farmers have become more efficient, yet efficiency gains tend to be absorbed by more irrigation, so overall caps on use are needed.
Water is underpriced, which encourages waste; trading water rights is one proposal, but it could harm small farmers.
Desalination and the reuse of treated wastewater can increase supply, although desalinated water is energy-intensive and costly.
Water transfers between basins generate growing political and legal conflicts between regions.
The EU sets environmental requirements for water and farm subsidies, while European demand for cheap produce indirectly draws on scarce water.
Farmers are adapting with new crops and techniques, but the future of southern agriculture depends on urgent decisions about prices, rights and priorities.

resumen_modelo: The report describes how recurring droughts in Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece are putting agriculture under severe pressure, a situation that scientists expect to worsen with climate change. Farming is the main consumer of water in Spain, mostly for irrigation, which, although limited to a small part of the farmland, generates much of the sector’s value and sustains rural employment. However, the expansion of irrigated land, sometimes based on illegal wells, has depleted aquifers, as illustrated by the threatened wetlands of Doñana. Farmers have adopted water-saving technologies, but they complain that efficiency cannot compensate for drastic cuts in their allocations. Moreover, experts point out that savings per plot often lead to more irrigated land, so that total use does not decline unless it is capped. Another key issue is the low price paid for water, which encourages waste; water markets are suggested, although critics fear they would benefit large firms. Increasing supply through desalination or the reuse of wastewater is also possible, yet costly in energy. Meanwhile, transfers between river basins fuel political disputes, and the European Union demands better protection of water resources. The article concludes that farmers are beginning to adapt, but that difficult decisions on prices, rights and priorities can no longer be delayed.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The farmers see the reappearance of the old village mainly as a tourist attraction.
preguntas.cita: the falling water level is not a picturesque curiosity but a direct threat to their livelihoods
preguntas.explicacion: Para los agricultores la bajada del agua no es una curiosidad pintoresca, sino una amenaza para su sustento.

preguntas.pregunta: What happened in some places during the drought, according to the text?
opciones: Farmers were paid to stop working
Drinking water had to be delivered by ship or lorry
Water prices were frozen across Europe
respuestas: Drinking water had to be delivered by ship or lorry
preguntas.cita: drinking water had to be brought in by ship or by lorry
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que en algunos lugares hubo que llevar agua potable en barco o camión. No habla de pagos a agricultores ni de congelación de precios, y los embalses no estaban llenos.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Irrigated land covers most of the cultivated area in Spain.
preguntas.cita: Irrigated land represents a minority of the cultivated area
preguntas.explicacion: El regadío es una minoría de la superficie cultivada, aunque genere una gran parte del valor de la producción.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 4 una palabra que signifique «humedales».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘areas of marshy land with lagoons’.
preguntas.cita: one of Europe’s most important wetlands
preguntas.explicacion: «Wetland» significa humedal; Doñana es uno de los más importantes de Europa.

preguntas.pregunta: What threatens the lagoons of Doñana, according to scientists?
opciones: Water extraction for nearby strawberry farms
respuestas: Water extraction for nearby strawberry farms
preguntas.cita: the extraction of water for nearby strawberry farms is drying up its lagoons
preguntas.explicacion: Los científicos atribuyen la desecación a la extracción de agua para los cultivos de fresa cercanos; el texto no menciona turismo, desaladoras ni trasvases en este caso.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 5 una expresión que signifique «riego por goteo».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘a system that waters plants slowly, drop by drop’.
preguntas.cita: We have invested in drip irrigation, sensors and everything the experts recommended
preguntas.explicacion: «Drip irrigation» es el riego por goteo, una técnica que ahorra agua en cada parcela.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the ‘rebound effect’ described in the text?
opciones: Prices rising again after a drought
Water savings being used to irrigate more land or thirstier crops
Reservoirs refilling quickly after heavy rain
Farmers returning to traditional dry crops
respuestas: Water savings being used to irrigate more land or thirstier crops
preguntas.cita: the savings are often used to expand the irrigated area or to switch to thirstier crops
preguntas.explicacion: El efecto rebote consiste en que el agua ahorrada se usa para ampliar el regadío o pasar a cultivos más exigentes, de modo que el consumo total no baja.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Critics fear that water markets could benefit large companies at the expense of small family farms.
preguntas.cita: Critics fear that such markets would favour large companies over small family farms.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto lo dice expresamente al presentar las críticas a los mercados de agua.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Most new desalination plants in Spain are financed by European funds.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto menciona que se construyen nuevas desaladoras, pero no dice nada de cómo se financian.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 8 una expresión que signifique «aguas residuales depuradas».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘used water that has been cleaned’.
preguntas.cita: The reuse of treated wastewater for irrigation is another option
preguntas.explicacion: «Treated wastewater» son las aguas residuales depuradas, que pueden reutilizarse para el riego.

preguntas.pregunta: In what sense do European consumers ‘import water’ from dry regions?
opciones: They buy bottled water from southern Spain
They buy fruit and vegetables grown with scarce irrigation water
They pay a water tax to southern regions
They finance water transfers between countries
respuestas: They buy fruit and vegetables grown with scarce irrigation water
preguntas.cita: European consumers continue to demand cheap fruit and vegetables all year round
preguntas.explicacion: Al comprar frutas y verduras cultivadas con regadío en zonas secas, los consumidores importan indirectamente el agua utilizada. Las demás opciones no aparecen.

preguntas.pregunta: Why does the farmer say that ‘efficiency is not enough’?
respuestas: Because even though he already uses much less water thanks to modern technology, a cut of half his water allocation leaves him unable to keep his trees alive. Efficiency cannot compensate for such a large reduction in available water.
preguntas.cita: But when the authorities cut our allocation by half, efficiency is not enough.
preguntas.explicacion: El agricultor ha invertido en eficiencia, pero los recortes de dotación son tan grandes que no bastan.

preguntas.pregunta: How are farmers adapting, and what does the author think must happen?
respuestas: Some farmers are trying crops that need less water, like pistachios or hardier olives, and techniques that reduce evaporation. The author believes that difficult decisions about water prices, rights and priorities must be taken now, without waiting for rain.
preguntas.cita: Some are already experimenting with crops that need less water
preguntas.explicacion: La conclusión combina la adaptación de los agricultores con la necesidad de decisiones políticas inmediatas.
